{{Short description|Differential variety}}
{{Distinguish|Diffeology}}

In [[mathematics]], a '''diffiety''' ({{IPAc-en|d|@|'|f|ai|@|,|t|i:}}) is a [[Geometry|geometrical]] object which plays the same role in the modern theory of [[partial differential equation]]s that [[algebraic varieties]] play for [[Algebraic equation|algebraic equations]], that is, to encode the space of solutions in a more conceptual way. The term was coined in 1984 by [[Alexandre Mikhailovich Vinogradov]] as [[portmanteau]] from '''diff'''erential var'''iety'''.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vinogradov|first=A. M.|date=March 1984|title=Local symmetries and conservation laws|url=http://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF01405491|journal=Acta Applicandae Mathematicae|language=en|volume=2|issue=1|pages=21–78|doi=10.1007/BF01405491|s2cid=121860845 |issn=0167-8019|url-access=subscription}}</ref>

==Intuitive definition==
In [[algebraic geometry]] the main objects of study ([[Algebraic variety|varieties]]) model the space of solutions of a system of algebraic equations (i.e. the zero locus of a set of [[Polynomial|polynomials]]), together with all their "algebraic consequences". This means that, applying algebraic operations to this set (e.g. adding those polynomials to each other or multiplying them with any other polynomials) will give rise to the same zero locus. In other words, one can actually consider the zero locus of the algebraic [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] generated by the initial set of polynomials.

When dealing with differential equations, apart from applying algebraic operations as above, one has also the option to [[Derivative|differentiate]] the starting equations, obtaining new differential constraints. Therefore, the differential analogue of a variety should be the space of solutions of a system of differential equations, together with all their "differential consequences". Instead of considering the zero locus of an algebraic ideal, one needs therefore to work with a [[differential ideal]].

An '''elementary diffiety''' will consist therefore of the ''infinite prolongation'' <math>\mathcal{E}^\infty</math>of a differential equation <math>\mathcal{E}\subset J^k(E,m)</math>, together with an extra structure provided by a special [[Distribution (differential geometry)|distribution]]. Elementary diffieties play the same role in the theory of differential equations as [[Affine algebraic variety|affine algebraic varieties]] do in the theory of algebraic equations. Accordingly, just like [[Algebraic_variety|varieties]] or [[Scheme_(mathematics)|schemes]] are composed of irreducible [[Algebraic_variety#Affine varieties|affine varieties]] or [[Scheme_(mathematics)#Definition|affine schemes]], one defines a (non-elementary) '''diffiety''' as an object that ''locally looks like'' an elementary diffiety.

== Formal definition ==
The formal definition of a diffiety, which relies on the geometric approach to differential equations and their solutions, requires the notions of jets of submanifolds, prolongations, and Cartan distribution, which are recalled below.

===Jet spaces of submanifolds===

Let <math>E</math> be an <math>(m+e)</math>-dimensional [[Differentiable manifold|smooth manifold]]. Two <math>m</math>-dimensional [[Submanifold|submanifolds]] <math>M</math>, <math>M'</math> of <math>E</math> are '''tangent up to order''' ''<math>k</math>'' at the point <math>p \in M \cap M' \subset E</math> if one can locally describe both submanifolds as zeroes of functions defined in a neighbourhood of ''<math>p</math>'', whose derivatives at ''<math>p</math>'' agree up to order <math>k</math>.

One can show that being tangent up to order <math>k</math> is a coordinate-invariant notion and an equivalence relation.<ref name=":0">{{Cite book|last=Saunders|first=D. J.|url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/geometry-of-jet-bundles/04672493C0263A1120B53A455A1AABED|title=The Geometry of Jet Bundles|date=1989|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=978-0-521-36948-0|series=London Mathematical Society Lecture Note Series|location=Cambridge|doi=10.1017/cbo9780511526411}}</ref> One says also that <math>M</math> and <math>M'</math> have same '''<math>k</math>-th order jet''' at <math>p</math>, and denotes their equivalence class by <math>[M]^k_p</math> or <math>j^k_p M.</math>

The '''''<math>k</math>''-jet space of <math>k</math>-submanifolds of <math>E</math>''''', ''denoted by '''<math>J^k(E,m)</math>''', is defined as the set of all <math>k</math>-jets of <math>m</math>-dimensional submanifolds of <math>E</math> at all points of <math>E</math>:'''<math display="block">J^k(E,m) := \{ [M]^k_p~|~p \in M,~ \text{dim}(M)=m, M \subset E \ \text{ submanifold} \}</math>'''As any given jet <math>[M]^k_p</math> is locally determined by the derivatives up to order <math>k</math> of the functions describing <math>M</math> around ''<math>p</math>'', one can use such functions to build local coordinates <math>(x^i,u^j_\sigma)</math> and provide '''<math>J^k(E,m)</math>''' with a natural structure of smooth manifold.<ref name=":0" />

[[File:Mathematical Jets.svg|thumb|<math>M</math> and <math>M'</math> have the same 1-jet at <math>p \in E</math> while <math>M</math> and <math>M' '</math> have the same 3-jet.]]

For instance, for <math>k=1</math> one recovers just points in <math>E</math> and for <math>k=1</math> one recovers the [[Grassmannian]] of <math>n</math>-dimensional subspaces of <math>TE</math>. More generally, all the projections <math>J^k(E) \to J^{k-1} E</math>  are [[Fiber bundle|fibre bundles]].

As a particular case, when <math>E</math> has a structure of [[Fibered manifold|fibred manifold]] over an <math>n</math>-dimensional manifold <math>X</math>, one can consider submanifolds of <math>E</math> given by the [[Graph of a function|graphs]] of local [[Section (fiber bundle)|sections]] of <math>\pi: E \to X</math>. Then the notion of jet of submanifolds boils down to the standard notion of [[Jet (mathematics)|jet]] of sections, and the [[jet bundle]] <math>J^k(\pi)</math> turns out to be an [[Open set|open]] and [[Dense set|dense]] subset of <math>J^k (E,m).</math><ref name=":1" />

===Prolongations of submanifolds===
The <math>k</math>-jet prolongation of a submanifold <math>M \subseteq E</math> is

<math display=block>j^k(M):M \rightarrow J^k(E,m), \quad p \mapsto [M]_p^k</math>

The map <math>j^k(M)</math> is a smooth [[embedding]] and its image <math>M^{k}:= \text{im}(j^k(M))</math>, called the '''prolongation''' of the submanifold <math>M</math>, is a submanifold of <math>J^k (E,m)</math> diffeomorphic to <math>M</math>.

===Cartan distribution on jet spaces===

A space of the form <math>T_\theta(M^{k})</math>, where <math>M</math> is any submanifold of <math>E</math> whose prolongation contains the point <math>\theta \in J^k (E,m)</math>, is called an '''<math>R</math>-plane''' (or jet plane, or Cartan plane) at <math>\theta</math>. The '''Cartan distribution''' on the jet space '''<math>J^k(E,m)</math>''' is the [[Distribution (differential geometry)|distribution]] <math>\mathcal{C} \subseteq T (J^k(E,m))</math> defined by<math display="block">\mathcal{C}:J^k(E,m)\rightarrow TJ^k(E,m),\qquad \theta\mapsto \mathcal{C}_\theta \subset T_\theta(J^k(E,m))</math>where <math>\mathcal{C}_{\theta}</math> is the span of all <math>R</math>-planes at '''<math>\theta \in J^k(E,m)</math>'''.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Krasil'shchik |first1=I. S. |url=https://zbmath.org/0722.35001 |title=Geometry of jet spaces and nonlinear partial differential equations |last2=Lychagin |first2=V. V. |last3=Vinogradov |first3=A. M. |date=1986 |publisher=Gordon and Breach Science Publishers |isbn=978-2-88124-051-5 |series=Adv. Stud. Contemp. Math., N. Y. |volume=1 |location=New York etc. |language=English}}</ref>

=== Differential equations ===
A '''differential equation''' of order <math>k</math> on the manifold <math>E</math> is a submanifold <math>\mathcal{E}\subset J^k(E,m)</math>; a '''solution''' is defined to be an <math>m</math>-dimensional submanifold <math>S\subset \mathcal{E}</math> such that <math>S^k \subseteq \mathcal{E}</math>. When <math>E</math> is a fibred manifold over <math>X</math>, one recovers the notion of [[Jet bundle#Partial differential equations|partial differential equations on jet bundles]] and their solutions, which provide a coordinate-free way to describe the analogous notions of [[mathematical analysis]]. While jet bundles are enough to deal with many equations arising in geometry, jet spaces of submanifolds provide a greater generality, used to tackle several PDEs imposed on submanifolds of a given manifold, such as [[Lagrangian submanifold|Lagrangian submanifolds]] and [[Minimal surface|minimal surfaces]].

As in the jet bundle case, the Cartan distribution is important in the algebro-geometric approach to differential equations because it allows to encode solutions in purely geometric terms. Indeed, a submanifold <math>S\subset \mathcal{E}</math> is a solution if and only if it is an [[integral manifold]] for <math>\mathcal{C}</math>, i.e. <math>T_\theta S\subset \mathcal{C}_\theta</math> for all <math>\theta\in S</math>.

One can also look at the Cartan distribution of a PDE <math>\mathcal{E}\subset J^k(E,m)</math> more intrinsically, defining<math display="block">\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}):=\{ \mathcal{C}_\theta\cap T_\theta(\mathcal{E})~|~\theta\in \mathcal{E}\}</math>In this sense, the pair <math>(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}))</math> encodes the information about the solutions of the differential equation <math>\mathcal{E}</math>.

=== Prolongations of PDEs ===
Given a differential equation <math>\mathcal{E}\subset J^l(E,m)</math> of order <math>l</math>, its <math>k</math>-th prolongation is defined as<math display="block">\mathcal{E}^k := J^k (\mathcal{E}, m)\cap J^{k+l}(E,m) \subseteq J^{k+l} (E,m)</math>where both <math>J^k (\mathcal{E}, m)</math> and <math>J^{k+l}(E,m)</math> are viewed as embedded submanifolds of <math>J^k (J^l (E, m), m) </math>, so that their intersection is well-defined. However, such an intersection is not necessarily a manifold again, hence <math>\mathcal{E}^k</math> may not be an equation of order <math>k+l</math>. One therefore usually requires <math>\mathcal{E}</math> to be "nice enough" such that at least its first prolongation is indeed a submanifold of <math>J^{k+1}(E, m)</math>.

Below we will assume that the PDE is '''formally integrable''', i.e. all prolongations <math>\mathcal{E}^k</math> are smooth manifolds and all projections <math>\mathcal{E}^k \to \mathcal{E}^{k-1}</math> are smooth surjective submersions. Note that a suitable version of [[Cartan–Kuranishi prolongation theorem]] guarantees that, under minor regularity assumptions, checking the smoothness of a finite number of prolongations is enough. Then the [[inverse limit]] of the sequence <math>\{ \mathcal{E}^k \}_{k \in \mathbb{N}}</math> extends the definition of prolongation to the case when <math>k</math> goes to infinity, and the space <math>\mathcal{E}^\infty</math> has the structure of a ''profinite-dimensional'' manifold.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Güneysu |first1=Batu |last2=Pflaum |first2=Markus J. |date=2017-01-10 |title=The Profinite Dimensional Manifold Structure of Formal Solution Spaces of Formally Integrable PDEs |url=http://www.emis.de/journals/SIGMA/2017/003/ |journal=SIGMA. Symmetry, Integrability and Geometry: Methods and Applications |language=en |volume=13 |pages=003 |doi=10.3842/SIGMA.2017.003|arxiv=1308.1005 |bibcode=2017SIGMA..13..003G |s2cid=15871902 }}</ref>

===Definition of a diffiety===

An '''elementary diffiety''' is a pair <math>(\mathcal{E}^\infty,\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}^\infty))</math> where <math>\mathcal{E}\subset J^k(E,m)</math> is a <math>k</math>-th order [[Diffiety#Differential equations|differential equation]] on some manifold, <math>\mathcal{E}^\infty</math> its infinite prolongation and <math>\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}^\infty)</math> its Cartan distribution. Note that, unlike in the finite case, one can show that the Cartan distribution <math>\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}^\infty)</math> is <math>m</math>-dimensional and [[Involutive distribution|involutive]]. However, due to the infinite-dimensionality of the ambient manifold, the [[Frobenius theorem (differential topology)|Frobenius theorem]] does not hold, therefore <math>\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}^\infty)</math> is not integrable

A '''diffiety''' is a triple <math>(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}),\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O}))</math>, consisting of

* a (generally infinite-dimensional) manifold <math>\mathcal{O}</math>
* the algebra of its smooth functions <math>\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O})</math>
* a finite-dimensional distribution <math>\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O})</math>,

such that <math>(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}),\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O}))</math> is locally of the form <math>(\mathcal{E}^\infty,\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{E}^\infty),\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}^\infty))</math>, where <math>(\mathcal{E}^\infty,\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{E}^\infty))</math> is an elementary diffiety and <math>\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{E}^\infty)</math> denotes the algebra of smooth functions on <math>\mathcal{E}^\infty</math>. Here ''locally'' means a suitable localisation with respect to the [[Zariski topology]] corresponding to the algebra <math>\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O})</math>.

The dimension of <math>\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O})</math> is called '''dimension of the diffiety''' and its denoted by <math>\mathrm{Dim}(\mathcal{O})</math>, with a capital D (to distinguish it from the dimension of <math>\mathcal{O}</math> as a manifold).

=== Morphisms of diffieties ===
A '''morphism''' between two diffieties <math>(\mathcal{O}, \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}), \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O}) )</math> and <math>(\mathcal{O}', \mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}'), \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O'}) )</math> consists of a smooth map <math>\Phi : \mathcal{O} \rightarrow \mathcal{O}'</math> whose [[Pushforward (differential)|pushforward]] preserves the Cartan distribution, i.e. such that, for every point <math>\theta\in \mathcal{O}</math>, one has <math>
d_\theta\Phi(\mathcal{C}_\theta) \subseteq \mathcal{C}_{\Phi(\theta)} 
</math>.

Diffieties together with their morphisms define the '''[[Category (mathematics)|category]] of differential equations'''.<ref name=":1">{{Cite book|last=Vinogradov|first=A. M.|title=Cohomological analysis of partial differential equations and secondary calculus|date=2001|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=0-8218-2922-X|location=Providence, R.I.|oclc=47296188}}</ref>

==Applications==

===Vinogradov sequence===

The ''Vinogradov <math>\mathcal{C}</math>-spectral sequence'' (or, for short, ''Vinogradov sequence'') is a [[spectral sequence]] associated to a diffiety, which can be used to investigate certain properties of the formal solution space of a differential equation by exploiting its Cartan distribution <math>\mathcal{C}</math>.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vinogradov|first=A. M.|date=1978|title=A spectral sequence associated with a nonlinear differential equation and algebro-geometric foundations of Lagrangian field theory with constraints|url=http://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?wshow=paper&jrnid=dan&paperid=41521&option_lang=eng|journal=Soviet Math. Dokl.|language=Russian|volume=19|pages=144–148|via=Math-Net.Ru}}</ref>

Given a diffiety <math>(\mathcal{O},\mathcal{F}(\mathcal{O}),\mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O}))</math>, consider the algebra of [[Differential form|differential forms]] over <math>\mathcal{O}</math> 

:<math>\Omega(\mathcal{O}):=\sum_{i\ge 0} \Omega^i(\mathcal{O})</math>

and the corresponding [[de Rham complex]]:

:<math>C^\infty(\mathcal{O}) \longrightarrow \Omega^1(\mathcal{O}) \longrightarrow \Omega^2(\mathcal{O}) \longrightarrow \cdots</math>

Its [[Cohomology group|cohomology groups]] <math>H^i(\mathcal{O}):=\text{ker}(\text{d}_i)/\text{im}(\text{d}_{i-1})</math> contain some structural information about the PDE; however, due to the [[Poincaré lemma|Poincaré Lemma]], they all vanish locally. In order to extract much more and even local information, one thus needs to take the Cartan distribution into account and introduce a more sophisticated sequence. To this end, let 

:<math>\mathcal{C}\Omega(\mathcal{O})=\sum_{i\ge 0}\mathcal{C}\Omega^i(\mathcal{O}) \subseteq \Omega(\mathcal{O})</math>

be the [[submodule]] of differential forms over <math>\mathcal{O}</math> whose restriction to the distribution <math>\mathcal{C}</math> vanishes, i.e.

:<math>\mathcal{C}\Omega^p(\mathcal{O}) := \{ w \in \Omega^p (\mathcal{O}) \mid w(X_1,\cdots,X_p)=0 \quad \forall~X_1,\ldots,X_p\in \mathcal{C}(\mathcal{O}) \}.</math>

Note that <math>\mathcal{C}\Omega^i(\mathcal{O}) \subseteq \Omega^i(\mathcal{O})</math> is actually a [[differential ideal]] since it is stable w.r.t. the de Rham differential, i.e. <math>\text{d}(\mathcal{C}\Omega^i(\mathcal{O}))\subset \mathcal{C}\Omega^{i+1}(\mathcal{O})</math>.

Now let <math>\mathcal{C}^k\Omega(\mathcal{O})</math> be its <math>k</math>-th power, i.e. the linear subspace of <math>\mathcal{C}\Omega</math> generated by <math>w_1 \wedge \cdots \wedge w_k,~w_i\in \mathcal{C}\Omega</math>. Then one obtains a [[Filtration (mathematics)|filtration]]

:<math>\Omega(\mathcal{O}) \supset \mathcal{C}\Omega(\mathcal{O}) \supset \mathcal{C}^2\Omega(\mathcal{O}) \supset \cdots </math>

and since all ideals <math>\mathcal{C}^k\Omega</math> are stable, this filtration completely determines the following [[spectral sequence]]:

:<math>\mathcal{C}E(\mathcal{O})=\{E^{p,q}_r,\text{d}_r^{p,q}\}\qquad\text{where}\qquad E^{p,q}_0 := \frac{\mathcal{C}^p\Omega^{p+q}(\mathcal{O})}{\mathcal{C}^{p+1}\Omega^{p+q}(\mathcal{O})},\qquad\text{and}\qquad E_{r+1}^{p,q} := H(E_{r}^{p,q},d_r^{p,q}). </math>
The filtration above is finite in each degree, i.e. for every <math>k \geq 0</math>

:<math>\Omega^k(\mathcal{O}) \supset \mathcal{C}^1\Omega^k(\mathcal{O}) \supset \cdots \supset \mathcal{C}^{k+1}\Omega^k(\mathcal{O})= 0,</math>

so that the spectral sequence converges to the de Rham cohomology <math>H(\mathcal{O})</math> of the diffiety. One can therefore analyse the terms of the spectral sequence order by order to recover information on the original PDE. For instance:<ref>{{Cite book|title=Symmetries and conservation laws for differential equations of mathematical physics|date=1999|publisher=American Mathematical Society|others=A. V. Bocharov, I. S. Krasilʹshchik, A. M. Vinogradov|isbn=978-1-4704-4596-6|location=Providence, R.I.|oclc=1031947580}}</ref>
* <math>E_1^{0,n}</math> corresponds to [[Action (physics)|action functionals]] constrained by the PDE <math>\mathcal{E}</math>. In particular, for <math>\mathcal{L}\in E_1^{0,n}</math>, the corresponding [[Euler–Lagrange equation|Euler-Lagrange equation]] is <math>\text{d}_1^{0,n} \mathcal{L}=0</math>.
* <math>E_1^{0,n-1}</math> corresponds to [[Conservation law|conservation laws]] for solutions of <math>\mathcal{E}</math>.
* <math>E_2</math> is interpreted as [[Characteristic class|characteristic classes]] of [[Bordism|bordisms]] of solutions of <math>\mathcal{E}</math>.
Many higher-order terms do not have an interpretation yet.

==== Variational bicomplex ====
As a particular case, starting with a fibred manifold <math>\pi: E \to X</math> and its jet bundle <math>J^k (\pi)</math> instead of the jet space <math>J^k (E,m)</math>, instead of the ''<math>\mathcal{C}</math>''-spectral sequence one obtains the slightly less general [[variational bicomplex]].
More precisely, any [[bicomplex]] determines two spectral sequences: one of the two spectral sequences determined by the variational bicomplex is exactly the Vinogradov ''<math>\mathcal{C}</math>''-spectral sequence. However, the variational bicomplex was developed independently from the Vinogradov sequence.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Tulczyjew|first=W. M.|chapter=The Euler-Lagrange resolution |date=1980|editor-last=García|editor-first=P. L.|editor2-last=Pérez-Rendón|editor2-first=A.|editor3-last=Souriau|editor3-first=J. M.|title=Differential Geometrical Methods in Mathematical Physics|chapter-url=https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007%2FBFb0089725|series=Lecture Notes in Mathematics|volume=836 |language=en|location=Berlin, Heidelberg|publisher=Springer|pages=22–48|doi=10.1007/BFb0089725|isbn=978-3-540-38405-2|chapter-url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Tsujishita|first=Toru|date=1982|title=On variation bicomplexes associated to differential equations|url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/osaka-journal-of-mathematics/volume-19/issue-2/On-variation-bicomplexes-associated-to-differential-equations/ojm/1200775039.full|journal=Osaka Journal of Mathematics|volume=19|issue=2|pages=311–363|issn=0030-6126}}</ref>

Similarly to the terms of the spectral sequence, many terms of the variational bicomplex can be given a physical interpretation in [[classical field theory]]: for example, one obtains cohomology classes corresponding to action functionals, conserved currents, gauge charges, etc.<ref>{{Cite web|title=variational bicomplex in nLab|url=https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/variational+bicomplex|access-date=2021-12-11|website=ncatlab.org}}</ref>

=== Secondary calculus ===
Vinogradov developed a theory, known as [[Secondary calculus and cohomological physics|secondary calculus]], to formalise in cohomological terms the idea of a differential calculus on the space of solutions of a given system of PDEs (i.e. the space of integral manifolds of a given diffiety).<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vinogradov|first=A.M.|date=1984-04-30|title=The b-spectral sequence, Lagrangian formalism, and conservation laws. I. The linear theory|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/0022247X84900714|journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications|language=en|volume=100|issue=1|pages=1–40|doi=10.1016/0022-247X(84)90071-4|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vinogradov|first=A. M.|date=1984-04-30|title=The b-spectral sequence, Lagrangian formalism, and conservation laws. II. The nonlinear theory|url=https://dx.doi.org/10.1016/0022-247X%2884%2990072-6|journal=Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications|language=en|volume=100|issue=1|pages=41–129|doi=10.1016/0022-247X(84)90072-6|issn=0022-247X|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book|url=http://www.ams.org/conm/219/|title=Secondary Calculus and Cohomological Physics|date=1998|publisher=American Mathematical Society|isbn=978-0-8218-0828-3|editor-last=Henneaux|editor-first=Marc|series=Contemporary Mathematics|volume=219|location=Providence, Rhode Island|language=en|doi=10.1090/conm/219|editor-last2=Krasil′shchik|editor-first2=Joseph|editor-last3=Vinogradov|editor-first3=Alexandre}}</ref><ref name=":1" />

In other words, secondary calculus provides substitutes for functions, vector fields, differential forms, differential operators, etc., on a (generically) very singular space where these objects cannot be defined in the usual (smooth) way on the space of solution. Furthermore, the space of these new objects are naturally endowed with the same algebraic structures of the space of the original objects.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Vitagliano |first=Luca |date=2014 |title=On the strong homotopy Lie–Rinehart algebra of a foliation |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0219199714500072 |journal=Communications in Contemporary Mathematics |language=en |volume=16 |issue=6 |pages=1450007 |doi=10.1142/S0219199714500072 |arxiv=1204.2467 |s2cid=119704524 |issn=0219-1997}}</ref>

More precisely, consider the '''horizontal De Rham complex''' <math>\overline{\Omega}^\bullet(\mathcal{O}) := \Gamma (\wedge^\bullet \mathcal{C(O)}^*)</math> of a diffiety, which can be seen as the leafwise [[de Rham complex]] of the involutive distribution <math>\mathcal{C(O)}</math>or, equivalently, the [[Lie algebroid#Lie algebroid cohomology|Lie algebroid complex]] of the Lie algebroid <math>\mathcal{C(O)}</math>. Then the complex <math>\overline{\Omega}^\bullet(\mathcal{O})</math> becomes naturally a commutative [[DG Algebra|DG algebra]] together with a suitable differential <math>\overline{d}</math>. Then, possibly tensoring with the normal bundle <math>\mathcal{V} := T\mathcal{O}/\mathcal{C(O)} \to \mathcal{O}</math>, its cohomology is used to define the following "secondary objects":

* '''secondary functions''' are elements of the cohomology <math>\overline{H}^\bullet(\mathcal{O}) = H^\bullet (\overline{\Omega}^\bullet(\mathcal{O}),\overline{d})</math>, which is naturally a commutative DG algebra (it is actually the first page of the ''<math>\mathcal{C}</math>''-spectral sequence discussed above);
* '''secondary vector fields''' are elements of the cohomology <math>\overline{H}^\bullet(\mathcal{O}, \mathcal{V}) = H^\bullet (\overline{\Omega}^\bullet(\mathcal{O} \otimes \mathcal{V}),\overline{d})</math>, which is naturally a Lie algebra; moreover, it forms a graded Lie-Rinehart algebra together with <math>\overline{H}^\bullet(\mathcal{O})</math>;
* '''secondary differential <math>p</math>-forms''' are elements of the cohomology <math>\overline{H}^\bullet(\mathcal{O}, \wedge^p \mathcal{V}^*) = H^\bullet (\overline{\Omega}^\bullet(\mathcal{O} \otimes \wedge^p \mathcal{V}^*),\overline{d})</math>, which is naturally a commutative DG algebra.

Secondary calculus can also be related to the covariant [[Phase space|Phase Space]], i.e. the solution space of the Euler-Lagrange equations associated to a [[Lagrangian field theory]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Vitagliano|first=Luca|date=2009-04-01|title=Secondary calculus and the covariant phase space|url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0393044008002039|journal=Journal of Geometry and Physics|language=en|volume=59|issue=4|pages=426–447|doi=10.1016/j.geomphys.2008.12.001|arxiv=0809.4164 |bibcode=2009JGP....59..426V |s2cid=21787052 |issn=0393-0440}}</ref>
